# Selection — TRD §15 row 4: the envelope wire format and batching granularity

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 4 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §7.2, §7.4, §13.2, §13.4, §12 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/envelope.json`](../../test/vectors/envelope.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-envelope-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-envelope-vectors.mjs)
**Amended by:** [`S0-4`](../review/remediation/S0-4/README.md) (2026-08-27) — three additions, none of them a
byte. The exact minted bytes are **persisted before the first network byte** in row 3's store at
`kind: 'outbound'`; the position is **reserved** before minting, because `seq` is inside both bound field lists
and two tabs would otherwise choose the same one; and the nonce budget's comparison reads positions **reserved**
under the generation rather than the raw `seq` — this row said _exactly as it does in §6.1_ and inherited that
section's defect along with its mechanism (TRD §§6.1/7.4).
**Companions:** [row 1](./row-1-algorithm-suite.md) selects the primitives; [row 3](./row-3-record-format.md)
established the binding conventions and the nonce argument reused here; [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) rides
beside this envelope and, as it turns out, dictates one of its fields.

---

## The selection

```
Clear header        what the relay validates (§7.2)

  v              1
  workspace_id
  credential_id
  epoch          the authorization epoch this envelope references
  gen            the content-key generation it is sealed under
  seq            this credential's own position — see §3
  nonce          12 bytes
  digest         SHA-256(ciphertext)

Sealed body         what the relay is not entitled to (§7.4)

  plaintext = LP("done/env-body/v1") || LP(actor_id) || LP(actor_kind)
              || u32be(count) || ( u32be(len) || update_bytes ) * count

  K_net = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = K_g, salt = "",
                      info = LP("done/envelope/v1") || LP(workspace_id), L = 32)

  AAD   = LP("done/env/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(credential_id)
          || LP(dec epoch) || LP(dec gen) || LP(dec seq)

  ct    = AES-256-GCM(K_net; plaintext, AAD)     tag included

Signature           covers both halves (§7.4)

  sig = Ed25519( device signing credential ;
          LP("done/env-sig/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id)
          || LP(credential_id) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(dec gen) || LP(dec seq)
          || LP(hex nonce) || LP(hex digest) )

Batching            one envelope carries one actor

  A batch closes at the first of:
    - a change of actor, credential, epoch or generation      (forced)
    - a flush interval, which must not be shorter than the
      acceptance-head cadence                                 (tunable, grounded)
    - a byte cap on the sealed plaintext                      (tunable, grounded)

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. This row is an encoding, and saying so narrows it usefully

§7.4 already decided the hard part and said it was a product constraint rather than a preference: workspace,
epoch, credential and update digest in the clear because the relay validates them; the attributed actor inside
the seal because the relay is not entitled to a per-write record of who wrote; the signature over both. **None
of that was open, and this row does not reopen it.**

What was open is the encoding, and the encoding turns out to contain one decision that is not an encoding at
all — §3. The rest follows row 3's conventions, which is the intended outcome: **the third carrier under one set
of binding rules should not need a third argument.**

---

## 2. Two bound field lists, because one of them structurally cannot do the job

Row 3's rule is that any cleartext field a reader trusts is authenticated. Applying it here runs into something
the storage carriers never hit: **two of the clear header fields cannot be in the AAD at all.**

| Field    | Why not in the AAD                                                                             |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `nonce`  | It is the AEAD's own input. Binding it inside its own associated data is circular              |
| `digest` | It is SHA-256 of the ciphertext that the AAD helps produce. Same circularity, one step further |

Both are fields a reader trusts, so leaving them unbound would be exactly the defect row 3 wrote its rule
against. **The signature is what covers them**, and that is the reason the signature message is a separate list
rather than "the header, again": it exists to reach the two fields the seal cannot.

**So the negatives come in two families, and this is not artificial.** A header field differing between what the
reader trusts and what was _sealed_ is one attack; differing from what was _signed_ is another. The vectors
mutate each field in one list at a time, leaving the other correct, which is both what the coverage audit needs
to isolate either and a fair model of the two attacks.

**The `digest` is of the ciphertext, not the plaintext**, because §7.2 has the relay validating it without a
content key. That makes the relay's cheap check and the client's real check the same value — and it is the value
[row 5](./row-5-finalization.md)'s accepted chain binds, so all three agree by construction rather than by three
compatible definitions.

---

## 3. `seq` is one number meaning two things, and row 5 is why it has to be

This is the decision inside the encoding, and it was not obvious until row 5 existed.

The envelope needs a position: row 5's chain is per credential and gap-free, and its links bind `n`. The
question is whether the client's own outbound counter and the service's accepted position are **one number or
two**.

**They are one, and it is forced.** Row 5's first client rule is _verify a head against the link you replayed
yourself, never against the link the head claims_. A client can only replay its own chain if it can compute each
position without being told — so a service-assigned position would mean the client cannot verify anything until
the service tells it where its own writes landed, which is the trust the rule exists to remove. **Two numbers
would quietly undo row 5.**

**What that costs, stated rather than discovered.** The client cannot skip. If an envelope at position 3 is
refused — a stale epoch is the ordinary reason — nothing at 4 or above can be accepted until 3 is resolved, so a
permanently unacceptable envelope stalls that credential's chain. Two things make this tolerable: the _position_
is stuck, not the _bytes_, so the client re-mints the content at the same position under the current epoch; and
the case where it genuinely cannot is a revoked credential, whose chain is finalized anyway.

**One thing this pins that would otherwise be discovered at a fork.** A refused envelope never reaches a client,
because a client only ever learns of accepted positions — so an honest resend at position 3 cannot look like
row 5's `forked-link-at-same-position` to anybody. That is worth writing down: the two mechanisms interlock, and
the interlock is invisible from either one alone.

**And `seq` earns its second job the way row 3's did.** Row 3 bounded a 12-byte random nonce's collision
probability with `seq`, under NIST SP 800-38D's 2³² ceiling, on the grounds that the condition was checkable in
one comparison against a field that existed for other reasons. **That argument transfers here unchanged**, and
conservatively: `seq` counts every envelope the credential ever sent, while the budget counts only those under
the current generation.

---

## 4. What the batch may contain, and what bounds it

§7.4 permits a source to batch **its own** mutations when actor, credential and epoch are the same. Two things
follow that the sentence does not say outright.

**Generation joins that list**, because the key changes with it; a batch spanning a rotation is not sealable.

**Batching costs no attribution granularity at all**, which is worth stating because it sounds like it should.
The actor is a single sealed field, so an envelope carries one actor by construction — merging two of the same
actor's updates loses nothing that was ever recorded per update. This is the property that makes batching a free
optimization rather than a trade against §7.4's attribution invariant.

**The two tunables have grounds, and the grounds are more useful than the numbers.**

- **The flush interval must not be shorter than the acceptance-head cadence.** Row 5 holds an envelope until a
  signed head reaches its position, so flushing faster than the service signs buys nothing at all — it produces
  more envelopes that wait the same length of time. That is a derived constraint rather than a chosen number,
  and it is the useful half.
- **The byte cap bounds one retained object.** §7.4 has a device retaining its own outbound envelopes back to
  the last admitted checkpoint, so the cap sets how coarse that retention is, not how large. It is not
  CPU-bound: §12 budgets envelope signing at 5 ms p95 off the edit path, and one AES-GCM seal plus one Ed25519
  signature is nowhere near that at any plausible size.

**Both numbers are starting values pending measurement**, on the same terms PRD §11 question 6 sets for the card
split threshold — a tunable, not a decision. Naming a number here would give it an authority the measurement
has not yet earned.

---

## 5. What §11.2 test 3 asks for, field by field

Test 3 is this row's conformance test, and it names six things: workspace id, actor, capability, epoch,
ciphertext and update digest. Five are bound directly. **The sixth is worth tracing, because it is bound
somewhere else and a reader could reasonably expect a field for it.**

| Test 3 names   | Bound by                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| workspace id   | The AAD, the signature, **and** the subkey's HKDF `info` — three, and the vectors separate them                                                                  |
| actor          | Inside the seal. Altering it is altering the plaintext                                                                                                           |
| **capability** | **No field.** Capabilities live in the epoch, bound to the credential (§13.5) — so `epoch` and `credential_id` together determine them, and both are bound twice |
| epoch          | The AAD and the signature                                                                                                                                        |
| ciphertext     | The AEAD tag, and `digest` under the signature                                                                                                                   |
| update digest  | The signature. It cannot be in the AAD — §2                                                                                                                      |

**"An envelope cannot be replayed into another workspace" has three independent refusals here**, and the vectors
keep them apart deliberately: `wrong-workspace-subkey` for the derivation, `aad-only-workspace_id` for the seal,
and `sig-only-workspace_id` for the signature. Row 2 established why that separation matters — a negative that
changes the derived key _and_ an authenticated field proves only that one of the two works.

---

## 6. What it costs

| Cost                 | Size                                                                                     |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Header, on the wire  | Two identifiers, four small integers, 12 nonce bytes and a 32-byte digest                |
| Ciphertext expansion | 16 bytes of tag, plus the body framing — one label, the actor, and four bytes per update |
| Signature            | 64 bytes                                                                                 |
| Client CPU, outbound | One AES-GCM seal, one SHA-256, one Ed25519 sign — async, off the edit path (§7.4)        |
| Client CPU, inbound  | One SHA-256, one Ed25519 verify, one AES-GCM open, against §12's 2 ms p95                |
| Relay CPU            | **One SHA-256 and one signature check.** No content key, no parsing of anything sealed   |
| Bundle               | **Nothing.** All four primitives are WebCrypto (row 1)                                   |

**The relay's cost is the line worth reading.** Its entire validation is a hash and a signature over a header —
which is what §7.2's "validates opaque envelope metadata" has to mean if the content-blindness boundary is real.
A format that required the relay to parse anything else would be negotiating that boundary rather than drawing
it, which is [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §7's named warning sign for Stage 4.

---

## 7. What Stage 4 owes, and what is not in this row

**The relay is replaced, not extended.** `relay/src/persistence.ts` calls `Y.applyUpdate` on load and
`relay/src/connection.ts` extends `Y.Doc`; under this format it can do neither, and §7.2 already says the gap is
a rewrite. This row is what the replacement validates against.

**Two smaller obligations.** An envelope that fails any check must be **refused and reported, never dropped
silently** — rows 2 and 3 both established that a path discarding what it cannot authenticate turns an
integrity problem into data loss, and the same rule applies at the network boundary. And the outbound retention
in §7.4 needs a floor expressed in positions rather than bytes, so it composes with row 5's replay; that is
row 6's, and this row hands it one number instead of two.

**Not in this row.** How deep a device retains its own envelopes is **row 6**. The checkpoint's construction is
**row 7**. The attribution-preserving representation that would let history be re-signed without re-signing is
**row 8** and §13.7, and nothing here weakens the rule it exists under. Awareness is outside the seal entirely
and always was (§7.7).

---

## 8. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-envelope-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and `pnpm check`
now runs it with the other ten.

**The primitive KATs are not here, and their absence is structural** — AES-256-GCM, HKDF, SHA-256 and Ed25519
are row 1's. What this file carries is composition.

**Four envelopes and twenty-one negatives.** A single 18-byte keystroke update; three updates batched from one
actor; an import attributed to the system actor, which is the case that shows the actor's kind is invisible to
the relay; and the same bytes under a rotated generation.

**Sixteen of the negatives are the two families**, one per bound field per list, and the remaining five are the
ones that are not field bindings: the wrong subkey, a signature by another admitted credential, a flipped tag, a
truncated ciphertext, and a header whose `digest` is not of the ciphertext beside it — which is the only one the
relay itself can catch.

**Nothing here needed a second pass**, and it is worth saying why rather than claiming credit for it.
[Row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) and [row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md) each needed one, for different
reasons: row 5 has two layers, so its lower-layer negatives cannot isolate a single field; row 9 had a negative
resting on a **string comparison**, which passes a coverage audit while testing no binding at all. **This
construction has neither property.** It is flat, and every refusal above is a primitive failing — a wrong tag, a
wrong signature, a wrong subkey. That is a fact about the format rather than about the care taken writing it,
and it is the cheapest thing a reviewer can confirm: **if any check here could be satisfied by comparing two
strings, it would be the wrong check.**
